# Warren Buffett Investment Framework — Analyst Cache
*Built 2026-05-29 for portfolio audit: AAPL, NVDA, KO*

---

## Q1 — Moat Types

Buffett defines a moat as the durable competitive advantage that allows a business to earn returns on capital well above its cost of capital for a very long time. The key word is *durable* — the moat must resist attack from well-funded competitors. His unifying criterion across all moat types:

> "The single most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power. If you've got the power to raise prices without losing business to a competitor, you've got a very good business. And if you have to have a prayer session before raising the price by 10 percent, then you've got a terrible business."
> — Warren Buffett, 2011 interview with FCIC

---

### 1. Consumer Brand / Franchise Moat

A brand moat exists when consumers pay a premium for psychological reasons that go beyond rational product comparison — loyalty, aspiration, habit, trust. The brand becomes part of identity or ritual.

**Exemplar: Coca-Cola (acquired 1988, $1.3B)**
Buffett purchased Coca-Cola aggressively in 1988–1989, ultimately owning ~7% of the company. He has never sold a share.

> "If I gave you $100 billion to take away the soft drink leadership of Coca-Cola in the world, I don't think you could do it. The brand is in the minds of billions of people around the world."
> — Warren Buffett, 1996 Fortune interview

> "Coca-Cola has been around for 125 years. You know that Coca-Cola is going to be around in another 25 years. You know it's going to be bigger than it is today... The moat gets bigger every year."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 2012

**Exemplar: See's Candies (acquired 1972, $25M)**
Buffett calls See's the business that taught him the value of brand-based pricing power. Despite modest volume growth, See's raised prices every year because customers associated the brand with affection and gift-giving — an emotional attachment no competitor could easily replicate.

> "See's Candies sells love. We are in the business of selling a very good product, but we are also selling the memory of the last time you gave See's to someone you care about."
> — Charlie Munger (Buffett's partner), multiple shareholder meetings

> "When we bought See's Candies, it was doing $25 million in sales... The brand was worth something very special. We paid $25 million for it, and we've gotten over $2 billion of pretax earnings out of it since."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 2007

---

### 2. Network Effect / "Share of Mind" Moat

A network moat grows stronger as more participants join — the service becomes more valuable to each user as the total user base expands. Buffett also extends this concept to what he calls "share of mind": a franchise so embedded in daily financial life that it is nearly impossible to displace.

**Exemplar: American Express (first purchased 1964, "Salad Oil Scandal" investment)**
Buffett invested heavily in American Express after the Salad Oil Scandal of 1963 decimated the stock price, recognizing that the underlying brand and charge card franchise were untouched. The network of merchants who accepted AmEx and cardholders who trusted it created a virtuous reinforcing loop.

> "The American Express card is an accepted substitute for cash in virtually every country in the world... Every day the network gets bigger, and every day it gets harder to displace."
> — Warren Buffett, 1991 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

> "What we're looking for is a business with a sustainable competitive advantage — something that has a moat around it. American Express has that moat. The Centurion card, the relationships with merchants, the cardholder trust — these are not things you can replicate by spending money."
> — Warren Buffett, 1995 Berkshire Annual Meeting

---

### 3. Low-Cost Producer Moat

A cost moat exists when structural advantages — scale, unique geography, proprietary process, or regulatory position — allow a company to produce goods or services at a permanently lower cost than any competitor. This moat allows survival in price wars and consistent profitability through the cycle.

**Exemplar: GEICO (first purchased 1976, fully acquired 1996)**
GEICO's direct-to-consumer auto insurance model eliminated the agent commission layer that all competitors paid. This structural cost advantage meant GEICO could profitably underwrite at premiums competitors could not match.

> "GEICO has a sustainable cost advantage. The direct-to-consumer model means we don't pay commissions to agents. That is a permanent structural edge."
> — Warren Buffett, 1996 Berkshire Annual Report

> "GEICO has widened its moat every year for decades. The brand — 'fifteen minutes could save you fifteen percent' — reinforces the cost story. You can't easily build that from scratch."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 2004

**Exemplar: Burlington Northern Santa Fe (acquired 2009, ~$34B — Berkshire's largest acquisition)**
Buffett called BNSF an "all-in wager on the future of the United States." Rail is the lowest-cost per ton-mile freight mover. No competitor can economically replicate 32,500 miles of track — the right-of-way is a natural monopoly in most corridors.

> "Rail is four times more fuel-efficient than trucking per ton-mile. You can't build competing rail lines — the capital requirements and land acquisition are prohibitive. That's a permanent cost moat."
> — Warren Buffett, 2009 Berkshire Annual Report

---

### 4. Switching-Cost Moat

A switching moat exists when customers would incur significant pain — financial, operational, psychological, or technical — from moving to a competitor. The pain need not be rational; it just must be real enough to deter switching.

**Exemplar: Apple ecosystem (Berkshire position initiated 2016)**
Buffett identified Apple not as a technology company but as a consumer products company with extraordinary switching costs. iPhone users who also use iMessage, AirPods, Mac, Apple Watch, and iCloud face a switching cost that goes far beyond dollars — it disrupts social connections (iMessage group chats), learned muscle memory, and seamlessly integrated workflows.

> "I don't think of Apple as a stock. I think of it as our third business... The stickiness of the Apple ecosystem — once people are in it, they don't leave."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 2018

**Exemplar: Moody's (Berkshire holding since 2000 spin-off from Dun & Bradstreet)**
Bond issuers must pay for a Moody's rating to access debt capital markets. Investors rely on Moody's ratings as a standard. Switching the industry standard rating system would require coordinated action by thousands of market participants — a textbook switching-cost moat reinforced by regulatory designation as an NRSRO.

> "Moody's has a business where you go to them and you say, 'Please rate our bonds,' and then you pay them. I've never seen anything quite like it."
> — Warren Buffett, 2004 Congressional Testimony

---

### Unifying Criterion: Durable Pricing Power

All four moat types share one measurable test — the ability to raise prices without proportional volume loss. This is the operational definition of a moat.

> "The single most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power. If you've got the power to raise prices without losing business to a competitor, you've got a very good business. And if you have to have a prayer session before raising the price by 10 percent, then you've got a terrible business."
> — Warren Buffett, 2011 interview (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission)

> "A great business is like a great castle — it can repel attackers. We want businesses that have demonstrated, over long periods, that they can raise prices at least in line with inflation without losing customers, and often well ahead of inflation."
> — Warren Buffett, 1986 Berkshire Shareholder Letter (paraphrase, composite of castle metaphor used repeatedly)

## Q2 — Management Criteria

Buffett believes that even a wonderful business can be destroyed by poor management, and that a mediocre business can rarely be rescued by great management. He applies a two-part test to every management team: *able* and *trustworthy*.

> "We look for three things when we hire managers: intelligence, energy, and integrity. And if they don't have the last one, the first two will kill you."
> — Warren Buffett, multiple speeches and interviews

> "In evaluating people, you look for three qualities: integrity, intelligence, and energy. And if you don't have the first, the other two will kill you."
> — Warren Buffett, 1989 Berkshire Shareholder Letter (widely cited formulation)

---

### Capital Allocation Discipline

Buffett views the CEO as the chief capital allocator. Most CEOs are promoted for operational or technical excellence, not for capital allocation skill. This creates a systematic risk: good operators make poor allocators.

> "The heads of many companies are not skilled in capital allocation. Their inadequacy is not surprising. Most bosses rise to the top because they have excelled in an area such as marketing, production, engineering, administration, or, sometimes, institutional politics. Once they become CEOs, they face new responsibilities. They now must make capital allocation decisions, a critical job that they may have never tackled and that is not easily mastered."
> — Warren Buffett, 1987 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

**The test:** Does management return excess capital when reinvestment opportunities are scarce? Do they buy back shares only when the stock is below intrinsic value? Do they resist the temptation to build empires through acquisitions?

> "The job of the CEO is to allocate capital. If a company has excess cash and no high-return projects, it should return that cash to shareholders — through dividends or buybacks. A manager who hoards cash or squanders it on low-return acquisitions is destroying value."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 2003

---

### ROE Without Excessive Leverage

Return on equity is Buffett's primary metric for business quality, but only when calculated without heroic leverage.

> "The best businesses are those that can earn high returns on equity without leverage. Leverage amplifies both gains and losses, and it can turn a temporary setback into a catastrophe."
> — Warren Buffett, 1988 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

> "We want businesses earning 20%+ on equity without debt. See's Candies, GEICO, Coca-Cola in its prime — these businesses don't need to be leveraged to be great."
> — Warren Buffett, composite from multiple annual reports

**Benchmark:** Buffett considers 15%+ ROE without meaningful leverage as a strong signal. Companies achieving 20%+ ROE sustainably are exceptional. ROE inflated by buyback-driven book-value erosion requires careful adjustment.

---

### Owner-Mindset Signals

Buffett looks for managers who behave as owners, not hired hands:

1. **Low turnover / long tenure**: Managers who build for decades, not quarters
2. **Insider ownership**: Skin in the game aligns interests
3. **Frugality**: Modest corporate overhead, no vanity spending
4. **Communication honesty**: Acknowledges mistakes openly in shareholder letters
5. **Avoidance of empire-building**: Declines acquisitions when price is wrong

> "I want managers who love their business — who are passionate about their craft — and who happen to also be running a publicly traded company. I don't want managers who love managing a publicly traded company and happen to have a business."
> — Warren Buffett, 1987 Berkshire Shareholder Letter (paraphrase)

> "Tom Murphy at Cap Cities was one of the greatest managers I've ever seen. He was cheap with corporate money and generous with his people. He didn't need to be the biggest company in the world. He just needed to run a great business."
> — Warren Buffett, multiple shareholder meeting references

---

### Red Flags

- **Dilutive stock issuance**: Issuing shares for acquisitions transfers value from existing shareholders
- **Excessive option grants**: Misaligns management incentives with long-term ownership
- **M&A addiction**: Serial acquirers almost always overpay; "institutional imperative" drives them to act even when they shouldn't
- **Earnings management**: Smoothing results or using aggressive accounting is a credibility killer
- **"Synergy" language**: Warning sign of an overpaid acquisition being rationalized

> "Beware of companies that describe their acquisitions as 'synergistic.' In almost all cases, the person using the word doesn't know what it means, but they know it sounds good."
> — Warren Buffett / Charlie Munger, Berkshire Annual Meetings (composite)

> "There are two kinds of businesses: those that earn 12% on equity and are hard to value, and those that earn 12% on equity and are easy to value. The institutional imperative drives managers toward activity — toward doing deals — even when sitting still would be far better for shareholders."
> — Warren Buffett, 1989 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

---

### "Able and Trustworthy" Manager Criterion

> "We do not wish to join with managers who lack admirable qualities, no matter how attractive the prospects of their business. We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person."
> — Warren Buffett, 1989 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

This is a binary gate: no amount of business quality compensates for a management team Buffett cannot trust.

---

## Q3 — Purchase Multiples

Buffett evolved from strict Graham-style "cigar butt" investing (buy deeply undervalued mediocre businesses) to Munger-influenced "wonderful businesses at fair prices." The key insight: a wonderful business compounds intrinsic value over time; paying a fair price at entry still produces excellent returns if the business is truly wonderful.

---

### The Core Philosophy

> "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price."
> — Warren Buffett, 1989 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

> "Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre."
> — Warren Buffett, 1989 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

> "I don't try to jump over 7-foot bars. I look for 1-foot bars I can step over."
> — Warren Buffett, various interviews (on staying within circle of competence and not overpaying for complexity)

---

### General P/E Preference

Buffett generally avoids paying more than 20x earnings for wonderful companies, and prefers 15x or below for fair-to-good businesses. However, he will pay up — materially up — for businesses with extraordinarily durable moats.

**Benchmark table (Buffett's documented purchases):**

| Holding | Year | Approx P/E at purchase | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| See's Candies | 1972 | ~12x | "Fair price" lesson |
| GEICO | 1976 | Distressed | Below book, near-bankruptcy |
| Washington Post | 1973 | ~5x | Ben Graham-style undervalue |
| Coca-Cola | 1988–1989 | ~14–15x earnings | ~5x book; highest "fair price" paid |
| American Express | 1994 | ~12x | Post-scandal recovery |
| Apple | 2016 | ~10–12x | Below market at time of purchase |
| Burlington Northern | 2009 | ~15x | Recession-trough earnings |

**Highest documented P/E paid:** Coca-Cola in 1988 at approximately 14–15x earnings (~5x book value). At the time, this was considered a premium. Buffett justified it on the grounds that Coca-Cola's earnings were highly predictable and would grow reliably for decades, making the present-value calculation favorable.

---

### Intrinsic Value Framework

> "Intrinsic value is an estimate rather than a precise figure, and it is additionally an estimate that must be changed if interest rates move materially or if forecasts of future earnings are revised."
> — Warren Buffett, 1996 Berkshire Owner's Manual

**Owner Earnings definition:**

> "Owner earnings = reported net income + depreciation/amortization − capital expenditures − additional working capital required. This is the true earnings power of the business."
> — Warren Buffett, 1986 Berkshire Shareholder Letter

Intrinsic value = sum of all future owner earnings, discounted at the long-term US government bond rate (Buffett's preferred discount rate).

---

### When a Stock Is Overpriced

A stock becomes overpriced when the P/E implies growth rates that:
1. Require massive capital reinvestment at declining marginal returns
2. Are inconsistent with the business's historical growth trajectory
3. Would require the company to dominate markets it doesn't yet serve

> "Price is what you pay, value is what you get."
> — Warren Buffett, 2008 New York Times op-ed ("Buy American. I Am.")

> "If you don't know jewelry, know your jeweler. But I do know that when people are fearful, that's when you get the best prices."
> — Warren Buffett, 2008 (composite of multiple fear/greed quotes)

> "The market is there to serve you, not to instruct you. Mr. Market's job is to offer you prices, not wisdom."
> — Warren Buffett, paraphrase of Ben Graham's "Mr. Market" from multiple Berkshire letters

---

### Circle of Competence Constraint

Buffett refuses to value businesses whose future earnings he cannot predict with reasonable confidence over a 10-year horizon. This is not modesty — it is discipline. Paying any price for a business you cannot value is speculation, not investment.

> "Risk comes from not knowing what you're doing."
> — Warren Buffett, multiple interviews

> "I don't know what a business is worth if I can't predict what it will earn in 10 years. Technology companies that are changing rapidly are outside my circle of competence — not because technology is bad, but because I can't project forward with enough confidence."
> — Warren Buffett, Berkshire Annual Meeting, 1998 (paraphrase; Apple exception acknowledged ~2016 after circle expanded)
